blocks.text: What bird is there that by its nature appears wondrous to men? Its beak serves it for a belly, and its eye is in its tail: that is, behind that belly which it has in its beak. From this belly, then, or sack, or trough, which hangs from the lower part of the beak, the bird may also have been called הכוס by the Hebrews, from chos, that is, vessel or cup; for כוס chos is a thoroughly established word for a vessel or cup. This conjecture is considerably supported by the passage of the Psalm we have cited, דמיתי לקאת מדבר הייתי ככוס חרבות, for it would best be rendered thus: I am become like a pelican of the wilderness, and I was as an onocrotalus of the desolate places. And so in the same verse these two birds would be joined, the pelican and the onocrotalus, which are so closely akin that even the most learned take them indiscriminately. Among these is Oppian in the Ixeutica, where to the πελεκίνῳ [pelekinō], that is, the pelican, is attributed a κόλπος [kolpos], a kind of pouch hanging in front of the breast, in which it stores all its food for a while. Also Jerome, for whom קאת in the passage of the Psalm is the pelican, but elsewhere the onocrotalus, as in Levit. XI, 18. Es. XXXIV, 11. and Sophon. II, 14. And Belon, book 3, chapter 2 of De Avibus, where the pelican, the platea and the onocrotalus are taken for the same bird. Moreover, onocrotalus of the desolate places would be said correctly. For Jerome teaches on Es. XXXIV. that this animal is accustomed to live in desert places. And on Sophon. II., that there are two kinds of onocrotali, one aquatic, the other of the wilderness. So also Isidore, book 12, chapter 7. Accordingly Damir, in the chapter البجع [al-bajaʿ] albugia, or On the Onocrotalus, in the section On eating it, concludes that it is indeed lawful, yet not by force of the general rule which grants Muslims the eating of all water birds: ان [col. 277] ذلك الوجة يجري في طاير لا يغارق الما وهذا يالغه ثم يغارقه [inna dhālika al-wajh yajrī fī ṭāyir lā yughāriq al-mā wa-hādhā yālighuh thumma yughāriquh] Because this reasoning runs (that is, this rule holds) [III, 19] for those birds which always remain in the water; but this bird at one time lives in the water, at another is separated from it; namely, so as to withdraw into the remotest wilderness. This too must not be omitted: the Psalmist compares himself to this bird on account of his constant complaints and laments. For there had preceded מקול אנחתי, by reason of the voice of my groaning my bones cleave to my flesh. Now the voice of the onocrotalus has something mournful and dreadful about it. Aelian, in the place cited above: Φθέγμα δὲ ἔχει καὶ μάλα ἀπηχὲς [Phthegma de echei kai mala apēches], It has a very discordant voice. Hence by the Greeks it was called ὀνοκρόταλος [onokrotalos], as if it brayed like an ass; and by some of the Arabs جمل الما [jamal al-mā], camel of the water, as if it bellowed in the manner of a camel. Hence Albertus: It emits a dreadful voice, sounding as it were like a horn. And Olaus: It makes a great cry like the bird botaurus, that is, the bittern, which with its voice imitates the bellowing of a bull. Finally, this bird cannot have been unknown to the Jews, since reliable writers attest that it is found around Antioch in Syria and Gaza in Eretz Yisrael, and that it is common in Egypt. It might be added that this is how it came about that כוס chos was rendered by the Greeks, whom the rest followed, as νυκτικόραξ [nyktikorax] instead of onocrotalus: because for כוס chos they read בום bum. These two words, though they differ enormously in sound, are nevertheless very similar in Hebrew script. Further, that the word בום bum signifies the little owl, and غراب الليل [ghurāb al-layl], raven of the night, that is, the night raven, at least among the Arabs, whose language is a dialect of Hebrew, we have amply proved above ^{a)}.
